source.title: Scaling Laws for Native Multimodal Models
source.authors: Mustafa Shukor; Enrico Fini; V. G. Turrisi da Costa; Matthieu Cord; Joshua Susskind; Alaaeldin El-Nouby

record.file_problem: Minor PDF text-extraction and layout artifacts; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling laws in native multimodal image-text models, extending text-model scaling measurements to a new training setting and modalities.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported validation-loss scaling fits, compute-optimal fits, mixture-dependent coefficients, and the reported 8B extrapolation evaluation. The paper also reports routing, expert-specialization, efficiency, and downstream SFT results; these do not directly test the claim versions about scaling-law loss or downstream predictability.
record.test_reason: The study fits Chinchilla-style loss laws, compute-loss exponents and compute-optimal N/D allocations on 457 native image-text models (0.3B–4B, about 1e19–1e22 FLOPs). It also tests an 8B extrapolation, all in a new multimodal setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also conclude that early fusion has no disadvantage versus late fusion when trained natively, that it trains more efficiently, and that MoE sparsity improves loss at equal inference cost. The sparse tokens-over-parameters conclusion is from the main text; Appendix C.7's wording points the other way.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a similar parametric loss law and compute-optimal fitting framework to Hoffmann et al., but applies it to native multimodal models and image-text validation sets. The paper estimates compute using its stated formulas and fits with L-BFGS and Huber loss, as well as log-space regression for some compute-optimal fits.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported coefficients vary by target data type, training-mixture proportions, and dense versus sparse architecture. The authors use L-BFGS with Huber loss and grid-searched initializations for the parametric fit; compute-loss exponents are fitted on interpolated lowest-loss frontiers.

fits_no_version.finding: After SFT at 1.5B, downstream ranking (early > late, MoE > dense) matches the validation-loss ranking.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining-loss rankings across architectures at fixed scale carry over to downstream SFT performance.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision
record.problems: The study itself says broader exploration of data mixtures is needed, the relationship between validation loss and downstream performance remains unclear, and extrapolation to extreme model sizes is an open question. Its sparse-model scaling study uses one routing configuration (top-1 with 8 experts).
record.rows_left_out: No version-linked scaling results were omitted. Other reported results, including fusion-efficiency comparisons, routing comparisons, expert specialization measures, and SFT task scores, were left out because they do not directly test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: No text-only language models are trained; all systems are native image-text models.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude; only about a 2.4x parameter extrapolation to one 8B model is tested.
A Kaplan-vs-Hoffmann comparison on text models; stability of the split beyond about 1e22 FLOPs.
Not tested: depth is fixed at 24 and only width is scaled.
Image-only or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer scaling.
No downstream trend over scale. SFT is reported for three configurations at the single 1.5B scale.
Bending away from a power law; training-schedule effects (one constant-plus-cooldown schedule only); comparison of published laws.

missing.what: Closed-form vs regression fit coefficients (a, b, d)
Per-target compute exponents for each mixture (e.g. image-caption −0.056 to −0.061)
Sparsity-aware scaling-law fit for the MoE (α=0.589, β=0.372)
Held-in prediction errors as the baseline for the 8B extrapolation

record.verdict_notes: One label above has a typo: its key 'row_ids' was mis-spelled. Intended row_ids for the V2 label: ["R22"]. V1 links were removed because the systems are multimodal. Text-only DCLM loss rows (R9, R14, R17) could arguably be read as V1 evidence, but here they come from multimodal-trained models. The compute range is about 3 orders of magnitude. Fits for L∝C^c exclude FLOPs ≤3e19. The Figure 2 caption says 250M tokens, while Table 6 says 2.5B–600B. The reader's limits_scope labels on V1 and V5 (coefficients vary) were dropped: varying coefficients do not contradict the same power-law form, and that variation is V7 evidence. The reader's V2 limits_scope was dropped because the authors' open question is an untested part, not a result.

versions.untested_parts: The tested systems are native multimodal models, not text-only language models; the study does not test every language-model setup.
Extrapolation is reported for an 8B model; extrapolation to extreme model sizes or orders of magnitude beyond the tested runs is not established.
The study does not compare Kaplan-style and Hoffmann-style fits across the original text-only setups; results are for its multimodal models and stated compute estimates.
No controlled sweep of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count is reported.
The study tests native image-text pretraining. It does not test image-only or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning scaling laws, or transfer scaling laws.
Downstream SFT scores are reported for model configurations, but the study does not test a downstream performance trend over scale or a quantitative relationship to pretraining loss.

The study shows coefficient differences across data mixtures and model/data targets, but does not test whether published text-only laws disagree because of parameter counting or fitting choices, or whether curves bend away from a single power law.
